To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

two fossil assemblage with Flinders-style preservation of Ediacaran macroscopic organisms were identified and studied in the White Sea region; these assemblages are similar in their taxonomic composition and differ only in their size-frequency distribution, which reflects the different stages of sea bottom colonization; on the basis of the size-frequency distribution, we have reconstructed the development stages of the benthos communities in the Ediacara Sea.

the Ediacaran fossil assemblages in the White Sea region display the variations of community structure of the benthos, reflecting seasonal colonization, immigration, and seasonal conditions of the microbial mats associated with the communities of Ediacaran organisms.

the Ediacaran fossil assemblages in the White Sea Basin are composed of two main communities of the bivalve-like and the frond-shaped Ediacaran organisms that were associated with the microbial mats of different thicknesses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
paleoecology of the Ediacara biota, which is one of the most important problems of the modern geosciences.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ediacaran macroscopic benthos of the White Sea Basin, in contrast to the other regions, was characterized by the presence of the two similar but different in composition fossil assemblages.
the fossil assemblages from the White Sea region represent the communities of Ediacaran bionetwork, which were characterized by a seasonal development of benthic communities.
the Ediacaran macroscopic communities of benthic organisms were characterized by high biodiversity, high abundance of sessile benthic organisms, and high abundance of mobile benthic organisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fossil assemblages from the White Sea region are not monotonous and represent the different stages of the sea bottom colonization by benthic Ediarcan organisms.
the fossil assemblages from the White Sea region represent the communities of benthic macrofauna of the Ediacara biota.
the Ediacaran communities of the White Seabasin were similar in structure to modern communities of the bivalve mollusks and polychaetes.
